title: Birbal and the pot of rice in the tree.
lines: This is a story from India, about Emperor Akbar and his clever friend Birbal.
It was winter.
It was cold in the city of Agra.
Very cold.
At night it even froze.
One morning Emperor Akbar and Birbal were walking by the lake near the palace.
The water was ice cold.
The emperor put his finger in the water.
Brrr!
He pulled his finger out quickly.
Birbal, said the emperor, I think nobody could stand in this icy water for a whole night.
Not even for all the gold in the world.
Birbal thought for a moment.
I think there is someone, Your Majesty, he said.
If someone is very poor and needs money, he can be very strong.
The emperor laughed.
All right then, he said.
Whoever can stand in the lake for a whole night will get a thousand gold coins.
The news spread through the city.
There was a poor man.
He had a wife and children.
They had almost nothing to eat.
The man thought: With a thousand gold coins my family can eat for a whole year.
I'm going to try.
That evening he went to the lake.
He stepped into the icy water, up to his waist.
The emperor's guards stood by the lake to keep watch.
It was so cold.
The man's teeth chattered.
His legs went numb.
But he thought of his children.
And he kept going.
Far away, high up on the palace wall, a little lamp was burning.
The man looked at the little lamp.
He thought: It's warm there.
There's light there.
He looked at that little lamp all night.
And all night he stayed standing.
When the sun came up, the man stepped out of the water.
He had done it!
The guards brought him to the emperor.
He stood in the water all night, Your Majesty, they said.
The emperor was amazed.
How did you do that?
he asked.
I looked at the little lamp on the palace wall all night, said the man.
That helped me.
The emperor frowned.
Ha!
he said.
Then you kept yourself warm with the palace lamp!
That's cheating.
You won't get any gold.
The poor man was so sad.
He went home with empty hands.
Birbal said nothing.
But he was angry.
What the emperor did was not fair.
The next day Birbal didn't come to the palace.
Not the day after either.
The emperor sent a messenger.
Where is Birbal?
The messenger came back.
Birbal says he is cooking, Your Majesty.
He'll come when his rice is ready.
The emperor waited.
One hour.
Two hours.
The whole day.
No Birbal.
In the end the emperor went to Birbal's house himself.
There he saw something very strange.
In the garden a little fire was burning on the ground.
And high, high up in a tree hung a pot, on a rope.
A pot of rice and lentils.
Khichdi.
Birbal was sitting under the tree, waiting.
Birbal!
called the emperor.
What are you doing?
I'm cooking khichdi, Your Majesty, said Birbal.
But that pot is hanging very high in the tree, said the emperor.
And the little fire is down here on the ground.
That rice will never cook like that!
Birbal stood up.
He smiled.
Why not, Your Majesty?
he said.
If a poor man can get warm from a little lamp far away on a wall, then surely my rice can cook from a little fire that is so close?
The emperor stood still.
He looked at the pot.
He looked at the little fire.
And then he understood.
He had been unfair to the poor man.
He was ashamed.
You're right, Birbal, he said.
I made a mistake.
He had the poor man brought to the palace at once.
He gave him the thousand gold coins.
And another thousand, to say sorry.
The man cried with happiness.
Now his family had enough to eat.
And the khichdi?
Birbal took the pot down from the tree.
He put it on the fire, the way it should be.
And that evening the emperor and Birbal ate a bowl of warm khichdi together.
It was the tastiest the emperor had ever eaten.
The end.
